newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: WOMEN, YOUNG SEEN ON VERGE OF LUNG CANCER EPIDEMIC.
newsitem.headline: WOMEN, YOUNG SEEN ON VERGE OF LUNG CANCER EPIDEMIC.

text.p: Increased cigarette smoking is set to cause an epidemic of lung cancer in the developed world among young people, especially women, a leading cancer specialist said on Wednesday.
"More young people are smoking than ever before, and half of these are female," Dr Desmond Carney told Reuters in an interview at the eighth world conference on lung cancer in Dublin.

"Ninety-five percent of lung cancer deaths are due directly to cigarette smoking, and the great fear we have is that we are facing an epidemic of this disease in young people, especially young women. Smoking is falling in the mature population, but children are taking it up in ever greater numbers."
In addition to chairing the conference, Carney is an oncologist at University College, Dublin, and secretary general of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer.
He said Britain, the United States and Ireland had the highest proportion of female smokers.

The disease is already the biggest cause of cancer deaths in the United States, with 170,000 new cases a year, and in most of Europe. Ten years ago it overtook breast cancer as the leading cause of cancer deaths among American women.
Carney said when he worked as an oncologist at the U.S. National Cancer Institute in Bethesda in 1976 it was rare to see women or younger people with the condition.
"Now in the U.S. it is the most common killer of women and it is not uncommon to see people in their 30s and 40s with this disease."

The five-day world conference, which ends on Thursday, has brought together more than 2,500 scientists, physicians and radiologists from 63 countries to look at ways of tackling the "silent disease", one of the hardest cancers to diagnose and treat.
Symptoms such as coughing up blood and repeated bouts of bronchitis and pneumonia are often not evident until the cancer reaches an advanced stage.
Currently only around 13 percent of people diagnosed with lung cancer survive for five years or more, compared to an average of 40 percent for cancers in general.
Carney said there was a "swell of optimism" compared with the last world conference three years ago in Denver, Colorado, mainly because of advances in cancer-fighting drugs used in chemotherapy.
He said there was evidence combinations of drugs were helping to improve quality of life, and making radiotherapy and surgery more effective by shrinking the size of tumours in advance.

Breakthroughs in understanding the action of genes in lung cancer promise the creation of a new generation of biotechnology drugs, while molecular biology holds out the hope of accurate screening for early signs of disease.
"By analysing sputum you could probably find changes suggesting the brewing or beginning of lung cancer," he said.
But behind the optimism, Carney remains angry with tobacco companies, which he said were now switching attention to the developing world, and the passivity of western governments.
"If we are to make progress in major eradication it has to be in the area of prevention," he said. "None of this would matter if people didn't smoke."
